title: What training does the ACCC expect in a consumer law compliance program?
description: What the ACCC's four compliance program templates require for consumer law training, the 2026 penalty settings and priorities, and where AS ISO 37301 fits.
shortAnswer: The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) recommends every business run a competition and consumer law compliance program. Its four scaled templates, written for section 87B court enforceable undertakings, require at least annual training for directors and for staff whose duties could involve a contravention, induction training for new starters, delivery by a qualified compliance professional or lawyer, and an annual review of whether the training is effective. The templates do not reference AS ISO 37301.
keyTakeaways: Compliance programs are voluntary unless imposed by a court or offered in a section 87B undertaking, but the ACCC recommends every business implement one as part of good governance.
The ACCC publishes four templates scaled from micro or very low risk businesses (Level 1) to large or high risk businesses (Level 4).
Levels 2 to 4 require competition and consumer law training at least once a year for relevant officers, employees, representatives, agents and all directors, plus induction for new starters.

For conduct on or after March 28, 2026, the maximum penalty for most Australian Consumer Law breaches by a corporation is the greater of $100 million, three times the benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover.
AS ISO 37301:2023 identically adopts ISO 37301:2021. It is a compatible management system framework, but the ACCC's templates do not cite it.
appliesTo: Businesses subject to the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, including the Australian Consumer Law in Schedule 2
Businesses offering or bound by a section 87B court enforceable undertaking
Directors, officers, employees, representatives and agents whose duties could involve a contravention
Compliance officers responsible for designing and maintaining the program

sections.heading: Is a consumer law compliance program legally required?

blocks.text: A compliance program is not a general legal requirement, but the ACCC recommends one for every business and courts or undertakings can make one mandatory. The ACCC's page on [implementing a business compliance program](https://www.accc.gov.au/business/compliance-and-enforcement/implementing-a-business-compliance-program) defines a compliance program as an internal system designed to identify and reduce the risk of breaching the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and to create a culture of compliance. It states that "the court may require a business to implement a compliance program if they breach the Act".

The ACCC also says it does not review individual compliance programs unless they form part of a court enforceable undertaking offered under section 87B of the Act to resolve a matter, and it does not give legal advice on program design. Its [undertakings page](https://www.accc.gov.au/business/compliance-and-enforcement/accepting-undertakings) notes that undertakings often require a business to implement a compliance program, and accepted undertakings are published on the section 87B register.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects ACCC guidance, templates, penalty information and 2026-27 priorities as at November 2026. The penalty amounts quoted apply to conduct on or after March 28, 2026; earlier conduct is subject to the maximums that applied at the time.

sections.heading: What do the ACCC's four compliance program templates require for training?

blocks.text: Each template sets a training floor scaled to the size and risk of the business. The ACCC says the templates were developed as annexures to section 87B undertakings but also give a useful framework outside that context, and that a small business facing high compliance risk may need elements from a higher level.

blocks.text: In the [Level 4 template](https://www.accc.gov.au/system/files/Level%204%20Compliance%20Program%20Template_2.pdf), paragraph 12 requires compliance training "at least once a year" for all officers, employees, representatives and agents whose duties could result in them being concerned with conduct that may contravene the relevant law, and for all executive and non-executive directors. Paragraph 13 adds awareness of the business's obligations to the induction of the same groups. Paragraph 7 requires everyone to be made aware of the compliance policy as part of staff training and induction.

sections.heading: How does the ACCC expect training effectiveness to be tested?

blocks.text: The templates require an annual review that reports specifically on whether staff training is effective, not just whether it happened. In Level 4, a review must be completed within one year of commencement and annually after that (paragraph 16.4), carried out by an independent reviewer who did not design or implement the program and is not a present or past staff member or director (paragraph 16.2).

The reviewer's compliance report must state "whether the Staff Training and Induction is effective, and if not, what aspects need to be further developed" (paragraph 17.3). A drafting footnote gives, as an example of a material failure, staff training not being conducted at least once a year. The compliance officer must give the report to the governing body within 14 days (paragraph 18), and the business must keep program documents for the undertaking period plus two years. The guide on [evidencing training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator) covers the evidence types that answer paragraph 17.3.

sections.heading: Which Australian Consumer Law risks should training cover in 2026-27?

blocks.text: Training content should follow the business's own risk assessment, weighted toward the conduct the ACCC has said it will prioritize. The ACCC's [2026-27 compliance and enforcement priorities](https://www.accc.gov.au/about-us/accc-strategy-and-priorities/compliance-and-enforcement-priorities) include:

items: misleading pricing practices in the supermarket and retail sectors
misleading pricing and claims in essential services, with a focus on energy and telecommunications
manipulative and false practices and unsafe consumer goods in digital markets
environmental and sustainability claims, with a focus on greenwashing
unfair contract terms, focusing on harmful cancellation terms, automatic renewals, early termination fees and non-cancellation clauses
consumer guarantees, with a focus on motor vehicles
product safety for young children, including button battery, infant sleep and toppling furniture standards
enforcement of the Scams Prevention Framework

blocks.text: The ACCC's [fines and penalties page](https://www.accc.gov.au/business/compliance-and-enforcement/fines-and-penalties) says unconscionable conduct, false or misleading representations and supplying unsafe or banned goods attract, for corporations, the greater of $100,000,000, three times the reasonably attributable benefit, or 30% of adjusted turnover during the breach turnover period, and $2,500,000 for individuals. Infringement notices are commonly $21,840 for corporations, $218,400 for listed corporations and $4,368 for individuals, based on the $364 penalty unit applying from July 1, 2026.

sections.heading: Where does AS ISO 37301 fit with the ACCC's expectations?

blocks.text: AS ISO 37301 is a compatible management system standard, not an ACCC requirement. Standards Australia's [AS ISO 37301:2023 listing](https://store.standards.org.au/product/as-iso-37301-2023) states that it "identically adopts ISO 37301:2021", records a publication date of February 17, 2023, and shows an amendment, AS ISO 37301:2023 Amd 1:2024.

The ACCC's templates do not cite AS ISO 37301; the only standard they name is AS/NZS 10002:2022 for complaints handling (Levels 3 and 4). A business certified to, or aligned with, ISO 37301 can still map its competence and awareness processes onto the template paragraphs above. The [ISO 37301 compliance training page](/regulations/iso-37301-compliance-training-requirements) explains the standard's competence requirements, and the [DOJ compliance program training expectations](/regulations/doj-compliance-program-training-expectations) page shows how a different regulator tests program effectiveness.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the business's consumer law obligations, risk assessment and roles as a structured framework, then links each role to the concepts and assessment points it must demonstrate. When the ACCC changes its priorities or a risk assessment is updated, the affected roles and assessments are identified from the framework, which supports the annual review question of whether training is effective. See [how to map training to compliance obligations](/guides/how-to-map-training-to-compliance-obligations).

faqs.q: Will the ACCC review our compliance program if we send it in?
faqs.a: No. The ACCC says it does not review individual compliance programs unless they are part of a court enforceable undertaking offered under section 87B of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 to resolve a matter. It also does not provide legal advice on compliance programs and suggests seeking legal advice.

faqs.q: Is annual consumer law training mandatory?
faqs.a: Only where a court order or undertaking requires it. Outside those cases, annual training is the ACCC's benchmark: the Level 2, 3 and 4 templates require training at least once a year for relevant staff and all directors, and treat missing annual training as an example of a material failure of the program.

faqs.q: Can a small business use the ACCC's free education program as its training?
faqs.a: The Level 1 template, designed for micro or very low risk businesses, uses the ACCC's Small Business Education Program as the training element for the director and permanent employees. The ACCC notes that small businesses facing high compliance risks may need elements from the larger business templates.

faqs.q: Does certification to ISO 37301 satisfy the ACCC?
faqs.a: The ACCC does not recognize certification as a substitute for its template requirements, and the templates do not reference AS ISO 37301. Certification can support the program, but a section 87B undertaking will still specify its own training, review and reporting terms.
